protections: Every member that unarchive extracts must resolve inside the per-archive output_dir (no '..' components, no absolute member names), for every extractor the module drives: 7z for zip/7z and tar for tar/bzip2/xz/gzip.
Containment must hold on resolved paths, so a symlink member (or a write through one) cannot place content outside output_dir (CWE-61), not only on the member-name string.
Recursive extraction of archives found inside an extraction must re-apply the same containment against the nested output directory (<output>/<member-stem>/).

Untrusted names turned into path components or archive entry names elsewhere in the repo (jadx output dir, postman_download workspace/collection names, apkpure app_id/attachment extension, docker_pull tag) must be sanitized before being joined to an output directory.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The report says Zip-Slip and the zip path is the 7z entry; tar is a different binary that already strips leading '/' and refuses member names containing '..', so the tar rows need no change.

The archive's member names contain no '..' and no leading '/', so a member-name check passes; the module never inspects link entries (no lstat/is_symlink/realpath anywhere in extract_file) and item.is_file() at the recursion follows links, so a lexical check looks sufficient.
Nested archives go straight back through the same extract_file(), so a guard placed there automatically covers them.
The advisory names the unarchive module; jadx is a separate, opt-in module (flags passive/safe/code-enum) that only decompiles APKs/XAPKs, so it is out of scope.
Workspace and collection names come from the Postman API, and this is archive creation rather than archive extraction, so it is not the unarchive route.
app_id comes from the app store event and the filename from APKPure's Content-Disposition, both treated as trusted provider data.
Docker tag grammar is [A-Za-z0-9_.-], so a tag returned by a registry cannot contain '/' or '..' and needs no containment check.
The nested-archive layout <output>/<member-stem>/ and the overwrite flags are existing, tested behaviour; a stricter containment rule must leave them untouched, so there is nothing to change here.

output_dir is computed right next to the file and created by the module itself, so validating that this directory sits under path.parent looks like the containment check; the actual write targets are archive members, which never appear as an object in the code.

masking: Once a lexical member-name check (no '..', no leading '/') is added for the zip/7z path and the tar rows, T3 (symlink members, resolved vs lexical) is the only remaining escape, so it becomes the live route only after T1/T2 are fixed.
T4 (nested recursion) is only reached when an extracted member is itself an archive; a guard placed only at the top-level call in handle_event (unarchive.py:54) never sees it.

conflicts.what: A containment rule that rejects any member name containing '/' or strips member directories breaks the module's own nested-archive contract (<output>/test/test.txt asserted at test_module_unarchive.py:165-168) and legitimate archives with nested paths.

Refusing every symlink member to obtain resolved-path containment refuses tarballs that legitimately ship symlinks and that the module extracts today, and must not disturb the --overwrite/-aoa behaviour (unarchive.py:19-26) that re-extraction relies on.

fairness_risks: The module test asserts recursive nested extraction lands at <output>/test/test.txt (test_module_unarchive.py:160-168); any rule that flattens, renames or refuses member subdirectories contradicts a must-keep behaviour.
Legitimate tarballs commonly contain symlink members; a blanket 'reject symlink members' security rule refuses an input shape real users need.
Dot-prefixed members (.config, .env, .bashrc) are normal archive content; a rule rejecting names starting with '.' would refuse legitimate input.

libmagic.py:54 maps application/x-tgz to 'tgz' while compression_methods (unarchive.py:18-27) has no 'tgz' entry, so filter_event (unarchive.py:36-40) silently refuses such files today; any tightening of the format allowlist must not widen that gap.

Overwrite flags (-aoa at unarchive.py:19,22 and --overwrite at 20,21,25,26) are needed when a destination path already exists; a rule that refuses to write over an existing entry breaks re-extraction.
gzip/bzip2/xz are single-stream formats whose member naming is decided by tar inside the stream; a rule requiring the member name to match the archive stem refuses legitimate inputs.

design.why: Five independent judgements with different reasons to dismiss. T1 is the described zip/7z surface (anchor, easy). T2 is the tar family driven from the same table but a different binary, dismissed with 'tar already refuses ..'. T3 is resolved-vs-lexical path semantics (symlink members), dismissed with 'the member names are clean'; it is the how-type mechanism MiMo tends to miss and it survives any name-based check. T5 is a second implementation of the same expand-an-untrusted-archive operation in jadx, which receives exactly the JAR/APK types unarchive refuses (unarchive.py:17,33; jadx.py:38) and has no containment or output-dir randomisation, dismissed with 'the advisory is about unarchive'. T9 is the coupled must-keep layout <output>/<member-stem>/ asserted by the module's own test, which an over-hardened rule breaks. This beats a design built on T4/T10/T7: T4 is covered automatically by any guard placed in extract_file (same fix site as T1/T2), T10 is a partial-check decoy closed by the same per-member guard as T1, and T7/T8 sit in unrelated provider modules whose data is not archive-driven. Caveat: one post-extraction resolved-path walk over output_dir would technically close T1/T2/T3/T4/T9 at once, so the stack only holds if the task scores pre-extraction validation per format plus the symlink case and the separate jadx implementation.
